contraindications: Chlordiazepoxide and diazepam: long-acting, with active metabolites that accumulate in severe liver disease; avoid.

output.summary: No interaction prevents prednisolone. Of the benzodiazepines, lorazepam and oxazepam suit severe liver disease; chlordiazepoxide and diazepam accumulate. All benzodiazepines can deepen hepatic encephalopathy: lowest symptom-triggered dose with monitoring of consciousness.
warnings: Lorazepam and oxazepam are glucuronidated without active metabolites and are preferred in liver failure; use the lowest symptom-triggered dose and monitor consciousness and respiration.
Phenobarbital: long half-life and hepatic metabolism; sedation can be prolonged in liver failure.
Prednisolone: raises blood glucose and infection risk; monitor glucose and screen for infection.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Glucose 64 mg/dL, potassium 3.0 mEq/L, magnesium 1.4 and phosphorus 1.8 mg/dL as metabolic co-precipitants; thiamine 28 nmol/L (low); WBC 18.6 and CRP 48; bilirubin 14.8 mg/dL, albumin 2.0 g/dL and INR 2.4 (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 29); ammonia 82 µmol/L supports but does not grade HE.
action_criteria.label: Core laboratory work-up: blood count, electrolytes, renal and liver function, glucose, INR, ammonia and CRP, with toxicology where alcohol or drugs are in question
action_criteria.rationale: Confirms liver dysfunction and identifies metabolic and infective precipitants; thiamine because a malnourished heavy drinker is at risk of Wernicke encephalopathy.

action_criteria.label: Blood cultures, two sets, before the first antimicrobial dose
action_criteria.rationale: Fever 38.4 °C, WBC 18.6 and tachycardia on prednisolone make infection a possible precipitant, so cultures precede the first antibiotic dose.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pyuria; no growth at 48 hours.
action_criteria.label: Urinalysis and urine culture before the first antimicrobial dose
action_criteria.rationale: Part of the infection screen of a febrile patient on corticosteroids before antibiotics start; a urinary source would change the antibiotic plan.

action_criteria.label: Chest radiograph in the infection screen: fever on prednisolone
action_criteria.rationale: Fever 38.4 °C with WBC 18.6 on prednisolone for alcohol-related hepatitis: infection is the commonest precipitant of overt HE and the lung a common source, and corticosteroids raise the infection risk [EASL_HE_2022] [EASL_ALD_2018]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No acute intracranial abnormality; mild diffuse cortical atrophy.

action_criteria.label: MRI brain with and without gadolinium
action_criteria.rationale: Fever, agitation and possible Wernicke encephalopathy in a malnourished heavy drinker leave diagnostic doubt that HE alone does not settle; MRI looks for Wernicke changes and other causes.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Generalized theta-delta slowing with superimposed beta activity and intermittent triphasic-like waves; no epileptiform discharges or electrographic seizures.
action_criteria.label: EEG
action_criteria.rationale: Diffuse slowing supports a metabolic encephalopathy and excludes non-convulsive seizures, a question raised by fluctuating, agitated confusion during alcohol withdrawal.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Prefers lorazepam or oxazepam to chlordiazepoxide or diazepam, which accumulate in severe liver disease, given symptom-triggered at the smallest effective dose while his level of consciousness is watched; prednisolone raises no interaction concern.
action_criteria.label: Check the benzodiazepine for alcohol withdrawal against severe liver disease and the current medicines (prednisolone, thiamine)
action_criteria.rationale: The choice of benzodiazepine for withdrawal depends on hepatic metabolism: long-acting agents with active metabolites accumulate in liver failure and deepen HE.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give scheduled or long-acting benzodiazepines; treat alcohol withdrawal symptom-triggered with the lowest effective dose of lorazepam or oxazepam and close monitoring of consciousness (EASL ALD 2018).
Do not prescribe opioids or other sedating drugs: they precipitate and prolong HE; for pain use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day.
Do not give glucose before parenteral thiamine in this malnourished heavy drinker: it can precipitate or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy.
Do not restrict dietary protein: malnutrition worsens HE and outcome (EASL 2022).
required_recommendations: Give thiamine 200 mg IV three times daily before any glucose, for possible Wernicke encephalopathy (malnutrition, heavy drinking, low thiamine), without waiting for the MRI (EFNS 2010).
Correct the hypoglycemia (glucose 64 mg/dL) with IV dextrose after the thiamine, and monitor capillary glucose closely until oral or enteral intake is established.

Replace potassium to 4.0 mEq/L or more, because hypokalemia increases renal ammoniagenesis, and replace magnesium (1.4 mg/dL) and phosphorus (1.8 mg/dL) intravenously, monitoring for refeeding syndrome as nutrition starts.

Lactulose 25 mL every 1-2 hours until at least two soft bowel movements, then titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022); avoid over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury.

Manage the alcohol withdrawal (CIWA 12) in a monitored bed with symptom-triggered lorazepam or oxazepam at the lowest effective dose, regular CIWA-Ar reassessment and close monitoring of consciousness, because benzodiazepines can deepen HE (EASL ALD 2018).

Treat fever on prednisolone as possible infection: after blood and urine cultures, start empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics and review them at 48 hours with the culture and chest radiograph results; reassess prednisolone if an infection is confirmed (EASL ALD 2018).
Blood and urine cultures are drawn before the first antibiotic dose, which is not delayed for them.
Calculate the Lille score on day 7 of prednisolone and stop it if the score is 0.45 or more (Louvet 2007).

Start nutritional support without protein restriction (35-40 kcal/kg and 1.2-1.5 g/kg protein per day, with a late-evening snack), by nasogastric tube if oral intake is inadequate (EASL ALD 2018; EASL 2022).
Once withdrawal has settled, start treatment for alcohol use disorder with addiction services and abstinence support (EASL ALD 2018).

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade II), severe alcoholic hepatitis on corticosteroids with underlying cirrhosis, with concurrent moderate alcohol withdrawal (CIWA 12) and hypoglycemia (glucose 64 mg/dL) as co-precipitants; high Wernicke risk given chronic alcohol use, malnutrition and low thiamine.

differential.key_features: Confusion 48 h after the last drink with tremor, diaphoresis, tachycardia and hypertension; CIWA 12 is moderate withdrawal. Concurrent rather than alternative: asterixis and fetor hepaticus indicate HE as well, which shapes the benzodiazepine choice; progression to delirium tremens (usually 48-96 h after the last drink) is the risk to monitor.

Heavy drinking with malnutrition and chronic pancreatitis plus altered mental state meet two Caine criteria; thiamine 28 nmol/L is low. A normal MRI does not exclude it; treat empirically with parenteral thiamine.
Glucose 64 mg/dL is a mild hypoglycemia that contributes but cannot explain the encephalopathy alone; corrected after thiamine.

Fever 38.4 °C, WBC 18.6 and CRP 48 on prednisolone; blood and urine cultures show no growth at 48 hours and the chest radiograph shows no consolidation, but fever and leukocytosis also occur with alcoholic hepatitis and withdrawal, and an occult infection on corticosteroids is not excluded by negative early cultures.
Prednisolone can cause neuropsychiatric symptoms but does not produce asterixis; two days of 40 mg makes it unlikely.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grade, evidence of liver disease and exclusion of other causes of altered mental status (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).

Child-Pugh C (12: bilirubin 14.8 3, albumin 2.0 3, INR 2.4 3, no ascites 1, HE grade II 2); MELD-Na 29 (creatinine 0.9, bilirubin 14.8, INR 2.4, sodium 131); Maddrey discriminant function 75 (prothrombin time 25.0 s against a control of 12.0 s, bilirubin 14.8 mg/dL).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection, GI bleeding, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia, hyponatremia), hypoglycemia, constipation, sedatives, alcohol and its withdrawal, dehydration and renal failure.

When HE and alcohol withdrawal coexist, scheduled or long-acting benzodiazepines worsen HE while untreated withdrawal risks seizures and delirium: treat symptom-triggered with the lowest effective dose of a short-acting agent without active metabolites (lorazepam or oxazepam) and monitor consciousness closely (EASL ALD 2018).

Thiamine is given before any glucose. Wernicke encephalopathy is a clinical diagnosis (two of four Caine criteria in people who drink heavily); MRI is insensitive and treatment does not wait for it (EFNS 2010).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Steroid neuropsychiatric effects are possible but do not cause asterixis and are not the primary driver here; the decision on prednisolone rests on the day-7 Lille score or on an uncontrolled infection.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute confusion to 'steroid psychosis' and abruptly discontinue steroids.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Give IV thiamine first, then correct glucose; this sequence avoids precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Reflexively give D50W to correct glucose first.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Asterixis and fetor hepaticus indicate concurrent overt HE; benzodiazepines deepen it, so withdrawal is treated symptom-triggered at the lowest dose of lorazepam or oxazepam rather than with a scheduled long-acting regimen.
red_herrings.data_point: CIWA 12 with tremor, diaphoresis and autonomic hyperactivity 48 hours after the last drink
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute all the confusion to alcohol withdrawal and start scheduled chlordiazepoxide.

metadata.difficulty_description: Overt HE (West Haven grade II) in severe alcoholic hepatitis on prednisolone, with concurrent alcohol withdrawal (CIWA 12), hypoglycemia and thiamine deficiency: overlapping conditions that need prioritized management
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 4 required actions (core labs with thiamine, blood and urine cultures, brain MRI) plus recommended EEG and benzodiazepine check; at least three overlapping problems (HE, withdrawal, Wernicke risk, hypoglycemia) and a benzodiazepine dilemma.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. K. is a 48-year-old man with severe alcoholic hepatitis on a background of cirrhosis (Maddrey discriminant function 75 on admission), admitted 2 days ago a few hours after his last drink and started on prednisolone 40 mg daily on admission per STOPAH trial protocol. He was brought to the neurology service today from the hepatology floor for acute worsening of confusion with agitation and tremor over the past 12 hours. He last drank 48 hours before this evaluation. On admission he was oriented and cooperative; now he is confused, combative, and diaphoretic. His CIWA score is 12, with tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, tremor, and hyperreflexia. He has no focal neurological deficits and no meningismus.
